items.stem: Machiavelli's point of view in the excerpt was most likely shaped by which of the following?

options.text: His service in a Florentine government weakened by factional strife and foreign invasions of Italy
options.label: key
options.why: The context line calls Machiavelli a former Florentine official. He served the Florentine republic from 1498 until the Medici returned in 1512, during the Italian Wars that began in 1494. That experience fits his view that loyalty breaks easily and fear lasts longer.

options.text: His reaction to Martin Luther's challenge to papal authority, which divided the German states into rival religious camps
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Machiavelli wrote the treatise in 1513. Luther's Ninety-five Theses came in 1517, and the German states split along religious lines later still.

options.text: His years as a court adviser to Emperor Charles V, who relied on Spanish troops and American silver to govern his lands
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Machiavelli never served Charles V. His career was in the Florentine government.

options.text: His humanist training, which led him to judge rulers chiefly by their piety and their adherence to Christian virtues
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt judges rulers by what keeps them safe, not by piety. It even ranks fear above love because men are base.

facts: Machiavelli served the Florentine republic as a government secretary from 1498 until the Medici returned to power in 1512.
The Italian Wars began with the French invasion of Italy under Charles VIII in 1494.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line identifies Machiavelli as a Florentine writer and former government official writing in 1513.
design.evidence_quote: Niccolo Machiavelli was a Florentine writer and former government official

items.stem: According to the excerpt, which of the following limits how a prince should use fear?

options.text: He must avoid being hated, which requires leaving his subjects' property and women alone
options.label: key
options.why: The last sentence says a prince can be feared safely as long as he is not hated, and that he avoids hatred by staying away from his subjects' property and women.

options.text: He must win the love of his subjects first, since bonds of obligation are the surest support of rule
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says the bond of obligation is broken at every opportunity. It treats fear, not love, as the more dependable support.

options.text: He must use fear only against foreign enemies and never against his own citizens and subjects
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt is about inspiring fear in a prince's own citizens and subjects. It does not limit fear to foreign enemies.

options.text: He must obtain the blessing of the pope, since only spiritual authority can make subjects fear punishment
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says nothing about religious approval. It ties fear to the dread of punishment.

facts: The Prince was written in 1513 and first printed in 1532, after Machiavelli's death in 1527.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The final sentence names avoiding hatred, by leaving subjects' property and women alone, as the condition for being feared safely.
design.evidence_quote: he can endure very well being feared whilst he is not hated, which will always be as long as he abstains from the property of his citizens

items.stem: Compared with medieval advice books for kings, Machiavelli's argument in the excerpt differed most in that it

options.text: judged a ruler's conduct by whether it kept him in power rather than by Christian morality
options.label: key
options.why: Medieval mirrors for princes urged rulers to practice Christian virtues. Machiavelli judges fear and love only by which is 'safer' for the prince. This secular, practical approach is a mark of Renaissance political thought.

options.text: argued that kings should be chosen by assemblies of nobles and clergy rather than by hereditary succession
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says nothing about how rulers are chosen. It is only about how a prince keeps his subjects' obedience.

options.text: insisted that a ruler's first duty was to defend the Church and punish heretics within his realm
options.label: reversal
options.why: This describes the religious duties that medieval writers stressed. It is not the secular concern with security found in the excerpt.

options.text: claimed that rulers held power by divine right and answered for their actions to God alone
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt does not base the prince's authority on God. It bases his security on fear of punishment.

facts: Medieval mirrors for princes advised rulers to govern according to Christian virtues.
The Prince (written 1513) is widely seen as an early secular, practical analysis of political power.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Machiavelli judges fear and love only by which is safer for the prince, not by moral or religious standards.
design.evidence_quote: it is much safer to be feared than loved

items.stem: Which of the following historical contexts best explains the excerpt's concern with how a prince can keep his subjects from turning against him?

options.text: Italian states faced unstable regimes and French and Spanish invasions after 1494
options.label: key
options.why: In 1513 the Italian states were fighting the Italian Wars, and Florence had seen its government change in 1494 and again in 1512. This instability helps explain the excerpt's focus on keeping a prince secure.

options.text: England and France were exhausted by the Hundred Years' War and by noble revolts over taxation
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Hundred Years' War ended in 1453 and was fought outside Italy. It does not explain a Florentine treatise of 1513.

options.text: German princes were seizing church lands after converting to Lutheranism in the 1520s and 1530s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These events came after 1513 and happened in the German lands, not in Machiavelli's Italy.

options.text: The Thirty Years' War had devastated central Europe and weakened the authority of the Holy Roman Emperor
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) began more than a century after the treatise was written.

facts: Charles VIII of France invaded Italy in 1494, beginning the Italian Wars.
The Medici were expelled from Florence in 1494 and returned to power in 1512.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 1513 date and the Florentine origin in the context line place the text in the period of the Italian Wars and Florence's changes of regime.
design.evidence_quote: men have less scruple in offending one who is beloved than one who is feared

items.stem: The excerpt's emphasis on a ruler's need to command obedience most closely parallels which development in western Europe in the late 1400s and early 1500s?

options.text: Monarchs in England, France, and Spain curbed noble power to strengthen royal rule
options.label: key
options.why: New monarchs such as Henry VII, Louis XI, and Ferdinand and Isabella brought their nobles under control and centralized authority. This matches the excerpt's interest in making a ruler's power secure.

options.text: The English Parliament asserted its supremacy over the crown and limited royal power by law
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Parliament established its supremacy in the seventeenth century, especially in 1688 and 1689. That was a limit on royal power, the opposite of strengthening it.

options.text: Church councils claimed authority over the pope, reducing papal power over the Western Church
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The conciliar movement peaked in the early fifteenth century. It was about authority within the Church, not a secular ruler's command of his subjects.

options.text: Dutch provinces rejected Spanish royal authority and formed a republic governed by their estates
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Dutch Revolt began in the 1560s. It was a rejection of royal authority, not an effort to strengthen it.

facts: Henry VII (r. 1485 to 1509) strengthened royal authority over the English nobility after the Wars of the Roses.
Ferdinand and Isabella, married in 1469, centralized royal power in Spain.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's focus on how a prince secures obedience through fear of punishment parallels the new monarchs' consolidation of power.
design.evidence_quote: fear preserves you by a dread of punishment which never fails

items.stem: The portraits of Ptolemy and Vespucci and the map's Latin title together suggest which of the following about the mapmaker's purpose?

options.text: To join the authority of ancient geography with reports from recent ocean voyages
options.label: key
options.why: The title names both the tradition of Ptolemy and the lustrationes (surveys or voyages) of Vespucci and others, and the two figures are shown as equal partners. The map combines classical learning with new information from the Atlantic voyages.

options.text: To reject classical geography by replacing Ptolemy's outdated picture of the world with new firsthand observations
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ptolemy is honored with a portrait and named in the title as a foundation of the map, so the map builds on classical geography instead of rejecting it.

options.text: To mark the papal line of demarcation dividing newly found lands between the crowns of Spain and Portugal
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the title, portraits or context links the map to the Spanish-Portuguese division of 1493 and 1494. The map was printed in Lorraine, not for either Iberian crown.

options.text: To give Portuguese pilots precise sailing directions for the route around Africa to the Indian Ocean
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The map is a printed twelve-sheet world cosmography with classical portraits, not a navigational chart, and nothing ties it to Portuguese pilots.

facts: Ptolemy's Geography, a second-century Greek work, was a major authority for Renaissance mapmakers.
Amerigo Vespucci made voyages to the coast of South America around 1499 to 1502, and accounts of them circulated in print.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The Latin title along the bottom and the paired portraits of Ptolemy and Vespucci show that the map draws on both ancient tradition and recent voyages.
design.evidence_quote: Universalis cosmographia secundum Ptholomaei traditionem et Americi Vespucii aliorumque lustrationes

items.stem: The production of this twelve-sheet map in Saint-Die in 1507 is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: The spread of printing presses across Europe after the mid-fifteenth century
options.label: key
options.why: The map is a printed work made in a small town in Lorraine about fifty years after Gutenberg. It shows how printing had spread and allowed maps and geographic knowledge to circulate in multiple copies.

options.text: The Protestant Reformation, which encouraged printers to issue works in vernacular languages for ordinary readers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Reformation began in 1517, ten years after this map was printed, and the map's captions are in Latin, not a vernacular language.

options.text: The publication of Copernicus's heliocentric theory, which led scholars to redraw the universe and the earth
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Copernicus published On the Revolutions in 1543, decades after 1507. The map also follows Ptolemy's tradition rather than a new cosmology.

options.text: The Peace of Westphalia's recognition of sovereign states, which prompted new maps of fixed borders
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Peace of Westphalia was signed in 1648, more than a century after this map was printed.

facts: Johannes Gutenberg developed movable-type printing in Mainz around 1450.
By 1500, printing presses were operating in many towns across Europe.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the map was printed in 1507 in Saint-Die, which places it in the spread of printing in the decades after Gutenberg.

items.stem: The placement of Ptolemy, an ancient Greek geographer, in a portrait in the map's top row most directly reflects which development?

options.text: The humanist revival of classical Greek and Roman texts
options.label: key
options.why: Renaissance humanists recovered, translated and studied ancient texts, including Ptolemy's Geography. Honoring Ptolemy on the map shows the authority these texts held for scholars around 1500.

options.text: The medieval Scholastic synthesis of Aristotle with Christian theology in universities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Scholasticism peaked in the thirteenth century and centered on Aristotle and theology. The Renaissance recovery of Ptolemy's Geography in Latin was a humanist project of the fifteenth century.

options.text: The Counter-Reformation's effort to defend Church authority through the Index of Prohibited Books
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Counter-Reformation and the papal Index came decades after 1507, and they have nothing to do with honoring an ancient geographer.

options.text: The Northern Renaissance painters' interest in realistic scenes of peasant life and landscape
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Northern artists did paint realistic scenes, but that does not explain why a mapmaker would honor an ancient Greek geographic authority.

facts: Ptolemy's Geography was translated from Greek into Latin in Florence in the early fifteenth century.
Renaissance humanism emphasized the recovery and study of classical texts.

design.key_evidence_in_source: A seated figure holding a globe appears in the top row under Ptolemy's name, and the title credits the tradition of Ptolemy.

items.stem: The European voyages to the lands across the Atlantic credited on this map most directly contributed to which development later in the sixteenth century?

options.text: Spanish conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires and silver mining
options.label: key
options.why: Voyages like those of Columbus and Vespucci opened the Americas to European expansion. Spain then conquered the Aztec Empire (1519 to 1521) and the Inca Empire (1530s) and developed silver mines such as Potosi (from 1545).

options.text: British territorial rule over Bengal through the East India Company's armies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: British rule in Bengal began after the Battle of Plassey in 1757, which is outside the sixteenth century and not connected to Atlantic voyages.

options.text: The abolition of the Atlantic slave trade by European powers concerned about labor
options.label: reversal
options.why: Atlantic contact led to the growth of the slave trade in the sixteenth century, not its abolition, which came in the nineteenth century.

options.text: Venice's rise to commercial dominance of Europe's trade with the Americas and Asia
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Atlantic voyages moved commercial power toward Atlantic states such as Spain and Portugal and later the Dutch Republic. They did not make Venice dominant.

facts: Hernan Cortes conquered the Aztec Empire between 1519 and 1521.
Silver was discovered at Potosi in 1545.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The title credits the voyages of Vespucci and others, and a strip of the lands across the Atlantic appears at the left edge, which points to the beginning of European expansion into the Americas.

items.stem: Which of the following would most limit a historian's use of this map as evidence of the actual coastline of the Americas in 1507?

options.text: The mapmaker worked in Lorraine from voyage reports, not his own travels
options.label: key
options.why: Waldseemuller produced the map in Saint-Die and drew on reports such as those credited to Vespucci and others. The map shows how European scholars interpreted secondhand accounts, so it is weak evidence of the real coastline.

options.text: The map was printed after Cortes conquered the Aztec Empire, so it exaggerates Spain's power
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The map dates from 1507, more than a decade before the conquest of the Aztec Empire (1519 to 1521).

options.text: The mapmaker drew the coastline from Indigenous informants who described only inland regions
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the title, credit line or context suggests Indigenous informants. The title credits European voyages.

options.text: The map was commissioned by the Spanish crown to hide its claims from Portuguese rivals
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The map was printed in Lorraine, and no source information connects it to a Spanish commission or to hiding claims.

facts: Martin Waldseemuller was a mapmaker working at Saint-Die in Lorraine who did not sail to the Americas himself.
Accounts attributed to Amerigo Vespucci circulated in print in the early 1500s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line places the mapmaker in Saint-Die in Lorraine, and the title says the map is based on the lustrationes of Vespucci and others, which shows it relied on secondhand reports.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between how Source A and Source B portray the condition of people living without government?

options.text: Source A sees it as a state of war, while Source B sees it as freedom bounded by a law of reason
options.label: key
options.why: Hobbes calls it a war of every man against every man. Locke calls it a state of perfect freedom within the bounds of a law of nature, which is reason.

options.text: Source A sees it as freedom governed by reason, while Source B sees it as a war of every man against every man
options.label: reversal
options.why: This swaps the two authors. The war image is Hobbes's, and the law of reason is Locke's.

options.text: Both describe it as an actual historical age that ended when the first Christian kingdoms were founded in Europe
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt dates the state of nature or ties it to Christian kingdoms. Both treat it as a condition to reason about.

options.text: Both argue that people in it hold no rights to their possessions, so property exists only by grant of a ruler
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Locke says people may dispose of their possessions and that no one ought to harm another's possessions. That is the opposite of this claim.

facts: Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651 and described the natural condition of mankind as a war of all against all.
Locke's Second Treatise of Government (1689-1690) described a state of nature governed by a law of nature known through reason.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source A's 'Warre... of every man, against every man' contrasts with Source B's 'state of perfect freedom... within the bounds of the law of nature.'
design.evidence_quote: The state of nature has a law of nature to govern it, which obliges every one

items.stem: In Source A, Hobbes claims that when people live without a common power to keep them in awe,

options.text: industry, trade, and learning cannot develop because their rewards are uncertain
options.label: key
options.why: Hobbes says there is no place for Industry because its fruit is uncertain. He then lists no navigation, no arts, no letters and no society.

options.text: people would cooperate freely in farming and trade, since reason teaches them not to harm one another
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This is closer to Locke's reasoning in Source B. Hobbes denies that there would be any Culture of the Earth or trade.

options.text: seaborne commerce would flourish because no government would collect customs duties on imported goods
options.label: reversal
options.why: Hobbes says there would be no navigation and no use of goods imported by sea.

options.text: the clergy would take on the task of keeping order and preserving the arts and letters of society
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt never mentions the clergy, and it says there would be no arts or letters at all.

facts: In Leviathan (1651), Hobbes argued that without a sovereign power, insecurity would prevent industry, agriculture, trade and learning.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Hobbes links the absence of a common power to the absence of industry, because its fruit is uncertain.
design.evidence_quote: there is no place for Industry; because the fruit thereof is uncertain

items.stem: Locke's view in Source B that people are naturally free, equal, and independent is most closely connected to which development in England in the late 1680s?

options.text: the Bill of Rights of 1689, which placed legal limits on the powers of the crown
options.label: key
options.why: Locke published soon after the Glorious Revolution. The 1689 Bill of Rights limited royal power, which fits his argument that power comes from free and equal individuals.

options.text: Charles I's personal rule of the 1630s, when he governed for years without summoning Parliament
options.label: reversal
options.why: Personal rule asserted royal prerogative rather than limits on the crown, and it came decades earlier.

options.text: the restoration of the Stuart monarchy in 1660, when Charles II was invited back to take the throne
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Restoration took place in 1660, not the late 1680s, and it brought back the monarchy rather than limiting it.

options.text: Oliver Cromwell's rule as Lord Protector in the 1650s, backed by the power of the New Model Army
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Protectorate was a 1650s military-backed regime. It came before the settlement that Locke's work came out alongside.

facts: The English Bill of Rights (1689) limited royal power after the Glorious Revolution of 1688-1689.
Locke's Second Treatise was published in 1689-1690.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line places Locke's work soon after the Glorious Revolution, and the text grounds political power in people's natural freedom and equality.
design.evidence_quote: being all equal and independent, no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions

items.stem: EXTRA. Hobbes's stress in Source A on continual fear and danger of violent death was most likely shaped by which of the following?

options.text: the collapse of royal authority amid the civil wars of the 1640s
options.label: key
options.why: Hobbes wrote during and after the English Civil War, when the breakdown of a common power was something he had lived through.

options.text: the Glorious Revolution, in which Parliament replaced James II with William and Mary
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Glorious Revolution took place in 1688-1689, after Leviathan was published in 1651. It shaped Locke's context, not Hobbes's.

options.text: the Spanish Armada's attempt to invade England during the reign of Elizabeth I
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Armada sailed in 1588, more than sixty years before Leviathan. It was not the disorder Hobbes was answering.

options.text: the Great Fear, a wave of peasant panic and revolt in rural France in the summer of 1789
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Fear belongs to the French Revolution, long after Hobbes's death.

facts: The English Civil War was fought from 1642 to 1651, and Charles I was executed in 1649.
Leviathan was published in 1651.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line dates Leviathan to 1651, just after the English Civil War, and the text dwells on fear and violent death.
design.evidence_quote: continuall feare, and danger of violent death

items.stem: EXTRA. Hobbes used the reasoning in Source A about life without a common power mainly to support which conclusion about government?

options.text: people should yield broad power to one sovereign to secure peace
options.label: key
options.why: In Leviathan, Hobbes argued that people escape the war of all against all by handing broad, undivided authority to a sovereign.

options.text: subjects keep a right to overthrow rulers who violate their lives, liberties, and estates
options.label: misattributed
options.why: A right of resistance to protect life, liberty and estate is Locke's position, not Hobbes's.

options.text: kings rule by divine right and answer to God alone, as Bishop Bossuet argued in France
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Hobbes based sovereignty on a contract made out of fear, not on divine right of the kind Bossuet set out for Louis XIV.

options.text: power should be divided among separate branches, as Montesquieu later proposed
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Separation of powers came from Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws (1748) and goes against Hobbes's call for undivided sovereignty.

facts: Hobbes argued in Leviathan (1651) for an absolute sovereign created by a social contract.
Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) proposed separation of powers.
Bossuet defended divine-right monarchy at the court of Louis XIV.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's claim that, without a common power to keep them in awe, people live in war supports Hobbes's case for a strong sovereign.
design.evidence_quote: during the time men live without a common Power to keep them all in awe, they are in that condition which is called Warre

items.stem: The overall trend in pig iron production shown in the table from 1865 to 1907 best illustrates which of the following developments?

options.text: The spread of heavy industry that ended Britain's early industrial lead
options.label: key
options.why: The table shows American and German output rising far faster than British output, which reflects the Second Industrial Revolution spreading heavy industry to rival states.

options.text: The revival of rural cottage production of metal goods under the putting-out system
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The putting-out system belongs to proto-industrialization before the factory age. Pig iron output on this scale came from large blast furnaces.

options.text: Britain's ability to keep its share of world iron output through free-trade policies
options.label: reversal
options.why: Britain's share fell over the period. By 1907 the United States and Germany both produced more than Britain did.

options.text: The shift of European industry from iron toward textiles as the leading growth sector
options.label: reversal
options.why: The shift actually went the other way: textiles led the first industrial revolution, and iron, steel and chemicals led the later phase.

facts: The United States passed Britain in pig iron output around 1890.
Germany passed Britain in pig iron output in the early 1900s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The rows for 1865 and 1907 show British output overtaken by the United States and Germany.
design.evidence_quote: Production of pig iron, 1865-1907 (thousands of long tons)

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence from the table would best support a claim that Britain lost its industrial preeminence between 1865 and 1907?

options.text: By 1907 both the United States and Germany produced more pig iron than Britain
options.label: key
options.why: Britain started the period far ahead, and being passed by both rivals in 1907 shows it had lost its relative position.

options.text: British output in 1865 was larger than that of the United States and Germany combined
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This figure is accurate, but it shows Britain's lead at the start of the period, not its later decline.

options.text: British pig iron output was larger in 1907 than it had been in 1865, showing steady growth
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Growth in absolute terms does not show a loss of preeminence. If anything, it qualifies the claim.

options.text: Germany's output rose faster than American output over the period covered by the table
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table shows American output growing much more than German output between 1865 and 1907.

facts: British pig iron output rose in absolute terms between 1865 and 1907 but was overtaken by the United States and Germany.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Students compare the 1907 row for the three countries with the 1865 row.

items.stem: The growth in German pig iron production shown in the table after 1870 is best understood in the context of which of the following developments?

options.text: Unification in 1871 and the annexation of the iron ore fields of Lorraine
options.label: key
options.why: Unification created a large national market, and the Treaty of Frankfurt (1871) gave Germany the iron ore fields of Lorraine, which fed its blast furnaces.

options.text: The Frankfurt Parliament's success in creating a unified liberal German state in 1848
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Frankfurt Parliament failed in 1848-1849. Germany was unified later, under Prussian leadership.

options.text: Napoleon's Continental System, which shielded German workshops from British imports
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Continental System dates from 1806 to 1814, decades before the period in the table.

options.text: Bismarck's sickness and accident insurance laws, which were passed to win workers away from socialism
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: These laws were real reforms of the 1880s, but they were a response to industrialization, not a cause of growth in iron output.

facts: Germany was unified in 1871.
The Treaty of Frankfurt (1871) gave Germany Alsace and part of Lorraine.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The German figures rise sharply in the rows after 1865.

items.stem: EXTRA: The shift in relative industrial strength shown in the table most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the decade before 1914?

options.text: Growing Anglo-German rivalry, including a race to build battleships
options.label: key
options.why: Germany's industrial rise made possible a fleet that challenged Britain, and the two powers competed over dreadnoughts after 1906.

options.text: Britain's repeal of the Corn Laws to lower food prices for urban industrial workers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846, long before the decade before 1914.

options.text: Britain's full abandonment of free trade in favor of high tariffs on German manufactured goods
options.label: overstated
options.why: Tariff reform was debated in Britain, but the country kept free trade until after the First World War.

options.text: The formation of the Holy Alliance to coordinate the great powers against revolution
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Holy Alliance was formed in 1815 under the Concert of Europe.

facts: Britain launched HMS Dreadnought in 1906, which intensified naval competition with Germany.
Britain kept free trade until the early 1930s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 1907 row shows Germany ahead of Britain.

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following is a limitation of the table for historians studying the social effects of industrialization in this period?

options.text: It records national output but says nothing about workers' wages or conditions
options.label: key
options.why: The table gives only tonnage by country. It cannot show living standards, working hours or labor conditions.

options.text: It omits the United States, the largest producer, so comparisons with Europe are skewed
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table does include the United States.

options.text: It was compiled before industrial production in Germany had begun to expand rapidly
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table was published in 1911, and its figures show German expansion already well under way.

options.text: It gives figures only in metric tons, which cannot be compared with British records
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The title says the figures are in long tons, and all countries are given in the same unit.

facts: The table appeared in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and reports pig iron output in long tons.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The title and context line show that the table measures only pig iron tonnage.
design.evidence_quote: the figures are thousands of long tons of pig iron
